title: Online Money Transfers vs. Banks: How Do They Compare?
summary: Compare online money transfer providers and banks for international payments. Learn what to check for fees, exchange rates, speed, and support.
body_markdown:
***Quick answer:** Banks and online money transfer providers can both help you send money internationally. Banks may let you arrange a transfer through an existing account, while providers such as[Remitly](http://www.remitly.com/) may offer different payment and delivery options. Compare the full quote, estimated arrival, limits, and recipient requirements for your specific transfer before choosing.*


**You already have a bank account. So why would you compare it to a service like Remitly before sending money abroad?**


**Because the fee you see first is rarely the whole story. The exchange rate, the recipient’s delivery options, the timing, and the amount that actually lands in someone’s pocket all shape the real cost of a transfer. Picking the right option means looking past the headline number.**


**Both banks and money transfer providers can move your money across borders. Each has its own process, its own pricing structure, and its own strengths depending on what you need. This guide breaks down how they compare, so you can make a confident decision for your specific transfer.**


## What is the difference between a bank transfer and an online money transfer service?


### Sending internationally through your bank


Banks may offer international wires through online banking, a mobile app, or a branch visit. The exact process depends on the institution. Some banks support international transfers only through a physical branch, while others let you submit a wire entirely online. Available currencies,[cutoff times](https://www.remitly.com/blog/money-transfer/international-wire-transfer-cutoff-times-for-major-us-banks/) , and required recipient information also vary by bank.


### Using a money transfer provider


With a provider such as[Remitly,](http://www.remitly.com/) you create an account, choose a destination and amount, enter your recipient’s details, and select from the available payment and delivery options for that transfer. The experience is built around digital self-service, though availability of specific features depends on the sending and receiving countries.


### Online transfers can still involve banks


It helps to clear up a common misconception: paying a money transfer provider from your bank account does not mean your bank arranged the transfer. A provider can deliver funds directly to a recipient’s bank account, but the sending and receiving processes are separate. “Online transfer” describes the experience of sending money digitally, not one single, universal payment network.


[According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_nprm_remittance-rule_2019-11.pdf) , remittance transfer terminology — including terms like “international money transfer” and “wire transfer” — is often used broadly by consumers, even though “wire transfer” has a narrower technical meaning involving a direct transfer between bank or credit union accounts. Understanding this distinction helps you compare your options more accurately.


## Online money transfer providers vs. banks at a glance


**What to compare** **Online money transfer provider** **Bank international-transfer service**

Use this table as a comparison checklist, not a guarantee of what every provider or bank offers. Confirm the specific details for your transfer before you send.


## Which option costs less?


### Look beyond the upfront transfer fee


A transfer’s true cost includes more than the fee listed at checkout. To compare accurately, factor in:


- The transfer fee itself
- The exchange rate applied to your transfer
- Any charges tied to your payment method
- Potential deductions by intermediary or receiving banks
- The total amount charged to you, the sender
- The total amount your recipient is expected to receive


Both banks and money transfer providers can generate revenue through currency conversion, not just through posted fees. A transfer advertised as “no fee” can still cost you through the exchange rate.


### Compare equivalent quotes


A reliable way to compare costs is to request quotes from both your bank and a money transfer provider around the same time, for the same transfer details. Record the following:


**Quote detail** **Bank** **Online provider**


Total paid in USD Enter quote Enter quote


Transfer fee Enter quote Enter quote


Exchange rate Enter quote Enter quote


Recipient amount Enter quote Enter quote


Additional deductions disclosed Enter details Enter details


Estimated arrival Enter estimate Enter estimate


If you use figures from actual quotes, note the date, amount, route, payment method, delivery method, and whether any promotional rate applied. A quote collected under one set of conditions won’t necessarily hold for a different transfer.


## Are online transfers faster than bank transfers?


Speed depends on the specifics of your transfer, not the type of institution you use. Several factors affect how quickly money arrives:


- How quickly your payment reaches the provider or bank
- Processing schedules and daily cutoff times
- Weekends and holidays
- Identity or transaction reviews required for compliance
- Availability of the recipient’s bank or payout provider
- The delivery method selected


It’s worth separating two things that often get conflated: how fast your payment is funded, and how fast your recipient actually receives the money. The same principle applies when comparing a bank wire to a money transfer — always check the specific arrival estimate shown for your transfer rather than assuming one method is categorically faster.


## Does your recipient need a bank account?


What your recipient needs on their end can determine which service makes the most sense for you.


### Bank-account delivery


If your recipient will receive funds in a bank account, confirm their full legal name, account details, receiving currency, and any required bank identifiers (such as a SWIFT code, IBAN, or local routing number) before you send.


### Cash pickup or mobile wallet


Some money transfer providers offer cash pickup or mobile wallet delivery for supported destinations. For example,[Remitly offers cash pickup](https://www.remitly.com/us/en/landing/cash-pickup) through a network of participating physical locations in select countries, giving recipients without a bank account a way to collect funds directly. Availability depends on the destination country, and recipients must meet any identification or wallet requirements tied to that delivery method. Not every bank requires a recipient to have an account, and not every provider offers cash pickup everywhere — check the options for your specific destination.


## How do security and consumer protections compare?


A few practical habits apply no matter which service you use:


- Check the provider’s identity and relevant regulatory registration.
- Use the official website or app, not a third-party link.
- Review your recipient’s details carefully before confirming.
- Understand the cancellation and error-resolution process before you need it.
- Check available support channels before sending.


Federal consumer protections for qualifying remittance transfers can apply to banks, credit unions, and nonbank providers alike. According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau,[coverage depends on whether the institution qualifies as a remittance transfer provider under federal law](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1005/30/) — generally, this includes any financial institution that handles more than 500 remittance transfers per year — not simply on whether the service is a bank or an app. This means a small bank with limited international transfer volume might not be required to provide the same protections as a larger bank or a dedicated remittance provider.


It’s worth noting that bank deposit insurance protects your account balance, not against transfer scams or unauthorized-payment losses. Protections for remittance errors and timely delivery are a separate matter governed by remittance transfer rules, not deposit insurance.


## When might your bank be a practical choice?


Using your bank for an international transfer can make sense when:


- Your bank supports the destination, currency, and recipient you need.
- Its quote is competitive for your specific transaction.
- You prefer to use an account you already have set up.
- You value in-person assistance at a branch.
- Your recipient’s instructions require a payment arrangement only your bank supports.


Not every bank offers the same service, so confirm these details apply to your specific bank and account before assuming they do.


## When might an online transfer provider be a practical choice?


A specialist provider may be worth considering when:


- Your recipient needs a cash-pickup or mobile wallet option your bank doesn’t offer.
- You want to compare a specialist’s quote against your bank’s offer.
- Your preferred payment method is available through the provider.
- The provider supports the amount, recipient, and delivery timing you need.


Each of these benefits depends on availability for your specific transfer. A provider isn’t guaranteed to outperform your bank in every case — comparing actual quotes is the only way to know for sure.

## Frequently asked questions (FAQs)


### Are online money transfers always cheaper than banks?


No. Whether a provider or a bank costs less depends on the specific transfer fee, exchange rate, and payment method involved. The only reliable way to know is to compare the full quote — not just the posted fee — for your exact transfer.


### Can I pay an online transfer provider from my bank account?


Some providers support funding directly from a bank account, depending on your location and eligibility. For example, Remitly offers ACH in the U.S., which lets eligible customers connect a bank account to fund a transfer without using a card. Availability varies by provider and market.


### Can an online transfer go directly to a bank account?


Yes, where the provider supports that recipient’s country and delivery method. Bank-account delivery is a common option for online money transfer providers, but you should confirm it’s available for your specific destination before sending.


### Which option is better for a large transfer?


Compare available limits, verification requirements, funding methods, recipient support, total cost, and delivery timing for your amount. Don’t assume banks or providers automatically offer higher limits — this varies by institution, account, and destination, so check the specific[send limits that apply to your transfer](https://www.remitly.com/us/en/landing/send-limits) .


### Can I cancel an international transfer?


Cancellation eligibility and timing vary by provider and by how far along the transfer is. Some remittance transfers can be canceled within a short window after submission, such as 30 minutes, while others may not be cancellable once funds are in transit or delivered. Review your receipt and contact the provider or bank promptly if you need to cancel.


## Choosing the right option for your transfer


**There’s no single right answer to the bank-versus-provider question — only the right answer for your specific transfer. Compare the amount your recipient will actually receive, the estimated arrival time, the available receiving options, the applicable limits, and the support you can access if something goes wrong. Doing this homework before you send puts you in control of the outcome, not just the upfront fee.**


*Fees, exchange rates, limits, payment methods, delivery options, and delivery estimates vary by provider and transaction. Review current quotes and applicable terms before confirming a transfer.*
